did_you_know.text: Did you know? This chapter describes a widespread Babylonian siege of Jerusalem: not only Nebuchadnezzar’s army fought against the city, but also the kingdoms and nations under his rule.
Did you know? Jeremiah prophesies to Zedekiah that he will be captured and brought before the king of Babylon, whom he will see and speak with face to face.

Did you know? Alongside his prophecy about Jerusalem’s fall, Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that he will not die by the sword, but will die peacefully and receive a mourning ceremony and an honorable burial like the kings who came before him.
Did you know? Lachish and Azekah were the last fortified cities still under Judah’s control during the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem.
Did you know? During the siege, Zedekiah made a covenant with the people to release their Hebrew male and female slaves, in accordance with the command given in the Torah.
Did you know? After the people released the slaves, they changed their minds: they took back the male and female slaves and enslaved them again.
Did you know? Jeremiah reminds the people that a Hebrew slave was to serve for six years and be set free at the beginning of the seventh year; however, their ancestors did not obey the LORD.
Did you know? The LORD describes setting the slaves free as the right thing to do, but returning them to slavery as an act that profanes his name.

Did you know? The covenant between the people and the LORD is symbolized by a calf cut in two, with those who passed between its pieces representing their acceptance of the covenant and their commitment to keep it.
Did you know? This chapter contains a play on the word “freedom”: because the people did not proclaim freedom for the slaves, the LORD proclaims “freedom” for them—to the sword, plague, and famine.
